item.title: Urban transport governance in Accra: Integrative approaches and hybrid modalities of reform
item.description:
Devanne Brookins
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261464899
Urban transport reforms, while recognized as central to economic transformation and environmental sustainability, have been difficult to realize across Global South cities. Engaging this challenge, the article explores the socio-institutional dynamics of urban transport reform through the lens of integrative approaches to governance in Accra. It argues that reform processes must be understood not merely as technical or efficiency-driven interventions but as moments of institutional disruption and political contestation that reveal the embedded interests, capacities, and power asymmetries among urban stakeholders. Focusing on hybrid governance modalities and their intersection with existing governing coalitions, the article highlights how such configurations reshape the role of the state and reconfigure relationships with non-state actors. Employing a political settlements framework, the analysis demonstrates how entrenched paratransit actors navigate and adapt to new institutional arrangements to maintain their influence, often to the detriment of transport reforms such as bus rapid transit. The case underscores the importance of historically informed and context-sensitive approaches to research and suggests the potential for comparative typology of integrative reforms to enhance understanding of institutional outcomes and inform future interventions. This article contributes to the growing literature on the governance of urban transport, offering a nuanced perspective of integrative approaches by revealing how integrative approaches, layered institutional innovations, and extant governing coalitions shape the uneven trajectories of urban transport reform.

item.title: Aspirations and expectations of participation in age-friendly cities: Perspectives from across four European case studies
item.description:
Patty Doran, Tine Buffel, Linda Naughton
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261493750
The Age-friendly Cities and Communities framework is widely used by policymakers seeking to create environments that support well-being and inclusion for older people as they age in place. However, there is limited empirical insight into how participation is understood and interpreted within age-friendly programmes. To address this gap, this paper examines how policymakers and delivery partners understand and approach older people’s participation through a multi-case study of four long-established European age-friendly cities: Brno, Oslo, Brussels and Bilbao. The case studies drew on semi-structured interviews ( n = 42) and observational fieldwork in each city, supported by in-country experts. The analysis identified four key themes: individualised participation linked to active and healthy ageing; civic and democratic engagement in decision-making; everyday participation in social and community life; and concerns around inclusion and exclusion. Findings show that participation is understood in multiple and sometimes competing ways, combining aspirations for inclusion and well-being with expectations that older people remain active and contribute to their communities. This reveals a tension between participation as an opportunity that older people can take up on their own terms if they wish to do so, and participation as an expectation associated with active ageing. The paper shows how such expectations can shift attention away from unequal opportunities to participate and the barriers faced by marginalised groups. The paper argues that, without critical attention to this tension, age-friendly participation risks reproducing rather than addressing inequalities.

item.title: Denser housing, more commodified? Comparing the relationship between densification and the production of (de-)commodified housing in Milan, Oslo and Vienna
item.description:
Michael Friesenecker, Marco Peverini, Rebecca Cavicchia
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261494806
Urban densification is often linked to sustainability benefits and sometimes advocated as a strategy to improve housing provision and affordability. This claim, however, rests on the assumption that increasing supply translates into improved housing affordability and social outcomes, while overlooking the fact that densification is often realised through market-led development processes that tend to reproduce commodified forms of housing provision. While decommodification cannot be equated with affordability, it is a relevant dimension of long-term inclusiveness of housing systems. We assume that the relationship between densification and the (de)commodification of housing is not inherent to increased density or housing supply but mediated by institutional and policy arrangements. This article explores how densification relates to the provision of (de)commodified housing through a comparative analysis of Milan, Oslo and Vienna, European cities with divergent housing systems and policy capacities. We combine quantitative analysis of tenure composition in densification areas with a qualitative assessment of capacities in land, zoning and housing policy. We show that housing produced through densification is predominantly commodified, but to varying degrees. In Oslo, private-sector-led land development and limited housing-policy capacity result in predominantly market-led densification; Milan combines greater planning capacity with limited subsidies and market-oriented land development while Vienna combines land provision and zoning with subsidies for limited-profit housing. Our comparative findings highlight that the degree of (de)commodification depends on local capacities to shape and coordinate housing and land policies towards either decommodified or market-oriented provision, demonstrating that similar densification strategies can produce different housing outcomes across institutional contexts.

item.title: Governance as obstacle: The reproduction of urban path dependencies in Kuwait
item.description:
Nuno F. da Cruz, Dhari S. Alrasheed, Muneerah Alrabe, Abdullah al-Khonaini
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261497864
This article investigates how urban governance in Kuwait reproduces unsustainable spatial and socio-economic outcomes. We distinguish two dynamics: outcomes the state deliberately sustains, above all the residential segregation of Kuwaitis and non-Kuwaitis, and outcomes it professes to pursue in its own plans yet persistently fails to deliver, such as curbing sprawl and car dependence or clearing chronic housing shortfalls. Situating governance within a rentier political economy, we treat it not as a neutral mechanism but as a state-spatial strategy through which oil rents are territorialised, with sharply different consequences for citizens and non-citizens. Drawing on interview-based network analysis, we show that authority is highly centralised yet fragmented in delivery and dominated by technocratic agencies, while actors focused on social or mobility concerns remain peripheral. While the government appears to acknowledge the need for reform, Kuwait’s governance regime actively obstructs the city’s ability to shift course, sustaining a path-dependent urban model through institutional exclusion, inertia, and repeated disruption of planning. The article contributes to debates on state capacity, rentier political economy, and urban governance in the Gulf, grounded in both quantitative and qualitative analysis.

item.title: Beyond ‘staying put’? Ageing in place through a relocation-based housing project in Singapore
item.description:
Shengxiao (Alex) Li, Shin Bin Tan
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261498093
Ageing in place (AIP) has become a central framework for planning housing and infrastructure in ageing societies. The AIP literature is dominated by the perspective of ‘staying put’. As such, there is limited evidence on whether relocation can provide a viable pathway for older people to age in place. Accordingly, this study examines Kampung Admiralty (KA) – a government-led vertical mixed-use development in Singapore that integrates senior housing, grocery shopping, healthcare, childcare, and an active ageing centre (AAC) under a single roof – to assess its potential as a strategy for promoting healthy ageing. From interviews with residents in KA and communities nearby, we find that relocating older adults to smaller, affordable housing units meets the needs of older people who want to downsize their residences. The AAC serves as a focal point for developing new social networks among both relocated residents and older adults living nearby. The ‘everything under one roof’ model is well received, especially given residents’ declining health and the challenges that Singapore’s tropical climate poses. Although KA demonstrates success in relocating people and integrating functions for older people, it has limitations, including insufficient provision for live-in helpers and constrained access to specialised healthcare. This case offers important theoretical and policy insights for AIP.

item.title: The project-ification of urban natures
item.description:
Charrlotte Adelina
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261498096
Project times are instrumental in co-producing temporalities of urban natures. To unpack how the figure of the project alters understandings of and governs relations with plant life, I point to frameworks through which urban ecologies come into being and are subsequently cared for. To illustrate these linkages, I draw on site visits to urban greening interventions in Hyderabad, Telangana (India) created as part of a state-led afforestation programme. In addition to a spatial ordering of plants for conservation, afforestation practices take shape through a ‘timing’ of vegetal life, in terms of projected and project gains. Taking the project-ification of plant life seriously, I argue that calls to recognise plural, divergent or non-linear temporalities would still need to contend with deeply entrenched, pervasive frameworks of project management in the governance of urban natures. Eco-managerial time practices and ways of relating to plants are, therefore, crucial sites of intervention for vegetal geography. Lastly, I question the uptake of the infrastructural lens, which interrogates how urban greening fails to perform its promised services without a critical look at the practices of doing, composing or contracting infrastructures, arguing instead for a study of ‘nature as project’.

item.title: Two-wheelers and bicycles: Comparing mobility, meaningful activities and well-being among urban-dwelling older adults in Bengaluru and the Northern Netherlands
item.description:
Louise Meijering, Sobin George, Thomas Aaron Lowe, Anne Mombarg, Aleida Antonia Rottink, Yashaswini SY, Prajwal Nagesh
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261498124
Mobility, or everyday movement, is an integral part of ageing well. Situated in theoretical frameworks around the capability to be mobile, meaningful activities and subjective well-being, this article zooms in on the role of health and the urban context in everyday movement. This article aims to contrast and compare how urban-dwelling older adults in different health conditions use their capability to be mobile to engage in meaningful activities that contribute to their experienced well-being in the Bengaluru Metropolitan Area and the Northern Netherlands. We draw on a qualitative study, combining activity diaries and in-depth interviews, collected among 18 older adults in the Northern Netherlands and 22 in Bengaluru. The findings show that in both contexts, engaging in independent mobility can contribute to engagement in meaningful activities and well-being, with a particularly important role for two-wheelers and bicycles. Specifically, we found that older adults can stay well, even when their health declines; that they are able to maintain their mobility in creative ways, in light of both individual and environmental challenges; and that they adapt both their capability to be mobile and to engage in meaningful activities. In conclusion, age-friendly environments should support the capability to move independently in later life.

item.title: Social isolation in motion: How socioeconomic segregation in everyday mobility varies by neighborhood racial-ethnic composition in U.S. cities
item.description:
Brian L. Levy
Urban Studies
DOI: 10.1177/00420980261493239
Recent scholarship finds that socioeconomic (dis)advantage in urban neighborhoods’ routine mobility networks—the neighborhoods their residents visit and receive visits from—predicts their vitality. Mobility-based (dis)advantage is correlated with, but conceptually distinct from, the socioeconomic status of a neighborhood’s residents. Thus, residential and mobility-based disadvantage can lead to distinct or compounding inequalities. This paper builds on Wilson’s social isolation framework to analyze how mobility-based disadvantage is unequally distributed by neighborhood racial-ethnic composition in the United States’ 100 most populous cities and their commuting zones. Majority-Black and majority-Hispanic neighborhoods experience heightened levels of mobility-based disadvantage, which deepens well-known disparities with majority-white neighborhoods based on residents’ socioeconomic statuses. Generally, mobility disadvantage compounds inequalities based on residential disadvantage, but for some Black and Hispanic neighborhoods with relatively low residential disadvantage, mobility disadvantage is a distinct form of inequality. The extent of these inequalities varies by urban form, with white spatial clustering and residential segregation by income as salient moderators. Isolation in structural neighborhood networks emerges as a clear feature of racial-ethnic inequality, though that one varies between cities.
